For our meta-regression, R-hat values for the model were all < 1.01, indicating convergence. There was significant heterogeneity between studies for bilingual single-language Figure 2 shows the network plot for the meta-analytic between-node effects. With respect to RQ1, bilingual conceptual vocabularies were not credibly different than their monolingual counterparts (g = -0.08 [-0.38, 0.21]), while single-language vocabularies were smaller than monolingual vocabularies (g = -0.78 [-0.97, -0.59]) and total vocabularies were larger than monolingual vocabularies (g = 0.85 [0.42, 1.28]).

Network meta-regression

Classical node-splitting analysis was not valid for our network meta-regression, as entering only non-redundant effect sizes meant that some comparisons (e.g., total versus conceptual vocabulary) had very few observations (because we preferentially recorded total versus monolingual and conceptual versus monolingual comparisons, even when total versus conceptual was theoretically available). As such, the indirect effects may be poorly estimated, and inconsistency between direct and indirect effects is likely. Instead, we compared the network-estimated effects with the direct effects (which have many observations) to assess consistency. Direct effects were estimated at -0.76 [-0.93, -0.59] (Δ g = -0.02 [-0.27, 0.25]) for bilingual single-language versus monolingual comparisons, 0.94 [0.49, 1.36] (Δ g = -0.10 [-0.68, 0.53]) for bilingual total vocabulary versus monolingual comparisons, and -0.06 [-0.34, 0.20] ( Δ g = -0.02 [-0.42, 0.38]) for bilingual conceptual vocabulary versus monolingual comparisons.

Publication bias

We used a comparison-adjusted funnel plot to assess for possible publication bias, as shown in Figure 3. As effect sizes depended on which vocabularies were under comparison, we adjusted the effect sizes by subtracting the comparison direct effect from each effect size to centre all effects on zero. Because we preferentially selected comparisons between bilingual and monolingual samples during data entry, we opted to only analyze effect sizes for bilingualmonolingual comparisons to avoid spurious effects (for within-bilingual comparisons). We conducted a Bayesian Egger's test, regressing comparison-adjusted effect sizes against their precision, such that small-study effects are indicated if the intercept is reliably different than zero (Chaimani & Salanti, 2012). Combining all three vocabulary measures, there was no overall indication of reliable small-study effects, b0 =¿ -0.44 [-0.89, 0.01]. Considering each vocabulary measure separately, single-language vocabularies showed a reliably negative intercept ( b0 =¿ -0.98 [-1.52, -0.44]), conceptual vocabularies showed a reliably positive intercept ( b0 =¿ 1.74 [0.71, 2.69]), and total vocabularies showed no reliable small-study effects ( b0 =¿ 1.37 [-0.05, 2.79]). We note that these asymmetries can be caused by genuine heterogeneity across studies and may not be a direct indicator of publication bias. Comparison-adjusted funnel plot of included effect sizes. Shaded areas indicate 95% and 99% confidence intervals respectively. Solid line indicates line of best fit. Dashed line indicates zero.

Covariate analysis

With respect to RQ2-6; Figure 4 shows an overview of the posterior estimates for each moderator in the meta-regression across all bilingual vocabulary measures. Age showed a positive effect for total and single-language bilingual vocabularies but not conceptual vocabularies; in other words, the difference between bilingual total vocabularies and monolingual vocabularies was greater for older children, and the difference between bilingual single-language vocabularies and monolingual vocabularies was less negative for older children, as shown in Figure 5A. We note that the age effect for total vocabulary may be driven by the BILINGUAL VOCABULARY META-ANALYSIS 20 small number of studies involving children older than 4 years of age, so we interpret these results with caution.

Figure 4

Posterior estimates of moderator effects on the difference between bilingual and monolingual vocabularies. Dashed line indicates zero. ASJP: Automated Similarity Judgment Program.

Vocabulary domain showed a consistent negative effect for all bilingual vocabulary measures, such that the difference between bilingual and monolingual vocabularies was more negative for expressive vocabularies than receptive vocabularies, as shown in Figure 5B.

Instrument type showed a negative effect for single-language vocabularies, such that the difference between bilingual and monolingual vocabularies was more negative for direct tools than indirect tools, as shown in Figure 5C. No reliable moderating effect of instrument type was found for conceptual or total vocabularies. We note that instrument type was correlated with age, with indirect tools primarily being used with younger children and direct tools primarily being used with older children, thus there may be shared variance in these two variables.

Language development status did not demonstrate any reliable effects, as shown in Figure 5D. However, it should be noted that there were relatively few effect sizes from atypical samples, and there were no effect sizes from direct contrasts between monolingual vocabularies and either conceptual or total vocabularies. Language distance, operationalized using ASJP distance, also did not demonstrate any reliable effects, as shown in Figure 5E. Again, we note that the limited variability in ASJP distance among observed language pairs (due in part to the highly skewed distribution over language pairs of the included studies) may have limited our ability to reliably detect any possible effects of language distance. Effect sizes for bilingual vocabularies compared against monolingual vocabularies, by (A) mean sample age in years, (B) vocabulary domain, (C) whether children are typically developing, (D) assessment type, and (E) language distance in terms of ASJP distance. Grey histograms indicate within-bilingual comparisons that could not be visualised in the main plots, but which were also included in the network meta-regression. Dashed line indicates zero.

Networks at representative covariate values

To better understand the contributions of the three moderators with reliable effects (age, vocabulary domain, and instrument type), we constructed post-hoc network plots at representative values of those covariates, holding the others at the grand mean (i.e., the mean across the entire dataset).

First, we looked at the effect of age, shown in Figure 6A. Observing the distribution over ages in the set of included studies revealed notable densities around 1-3 years of age and around 4-6 years of age; thus, we selected representative ages at the midpoints of those two ranges. At 2 years, bilingual conceptual and total vocabularies appeared to be indistinguishable from each other, and also from monolingual comparisons; however, by 5 years, only bilingual conceptual vocabularies were not reliably different than monolingual vocabularies, as total vocabularies reliably exceeded both conceptual and monolingual vocabularies. We also note that data beyond 6 years of age were very sparse for conceptual and total vocabularies, highlighting an underexplored area of research in bilingualism across development.

Next, we looked at the effects of vocabulary domain and instrument type, shown in Figure 6B and C. These networks showed a similar trend overall, with conceptual vocabularies being consistently the most similar to monolingual vocabularies. For comparisons between single-language and monolingual vocabularies, measuring receptive vocabularies (rather than expressive) and indirect measurements (rather than direct) seem to result in smaller effect sizes, whereas they appear to result in larger effect sizes between total and monolingual vocabularies. Discussion

When measuring the vocabulary abilities of bilingual children, what type of vocabulary measure is the most appropriate? Our network meta-analysis aimed to synthesize evidence toward this broad question by integrating vocabulary data from studies of bilinguals, incorporating over 50,000 children from 1288 observations arranged into 782 pairwise contrasts, which is to our knowledge currently the largest meta-analysis of bilingual children. Addressing RQ1, our results highlight how single-language, conceptual, and total vocabularies vary in their dissimilarity to monolingual comparison groups, with bilingual conceptual vocabularies being the most similar to monolingual counterparts, whereas single-language vocabularies are smaller and total vocabularies are larger than monolingual vocabularies.

We also found that the comparisons between bilingual and monolingual vocabularies differ according to features of the child and features of the measurement. Addressing RQ2, we found that total vocabularies diverge from monolingual vocabularies for older children, while single-language vocabularies diverged from monolingual vocabularies for younger children.

Addressing RQ3 and RQ4, we found that expressive vocabularies showed more negative effect sizes than receptive, and direct measures also showed more negative effect sizes than indirect for single-language vocabularies. However, addressing RQ5 and RQ6, we found no moderating effects of language development status or language distance; nonetheless, the stark imbalances in the distributions of those moderators in our dataset limits our ability to draw strong conclusions about the lack of moderation.

The similarity between bilingual conceptual vocabularies and monolingual vocabularies may suggest that these two measurements index the same underlying capacity in both groups.

For a monolingual child, the number of words known and the number of lexical concepts labelled are approximately the same. For a bilingual child, conceptual scoring gets at a comparable quantity, whereas total scoring counts translation equivalents twice, while singlelanguage scoring fails to capture part of the child's lexical knowledge (Bedore et al., 2005; Pearson et al., 1993). Given that total and conceptual scores differ in only how translation equivalents are counted, the growing gap across age between bilingual total and monolingual vocabularies is compatible with children adding additional second labels for concepts they already know in one language, although this theory should be interpreted with caution because our data do not allow us to test this idea directly. Additionally, instruments vary with respect to the number of possible translation equivalent pairs they can capture-some instruments are designed to be parallel, with all possible translation equivalent pairs included (e.g., De Anda et al., 2022), whereas other instruments may have been separately adapted into different languages, and thus may underestimate the number of translation equivalent pairs known by a child. Furthermore, vocabulary measurements are often important components of causal and statistical inference in cognitive development (e.g., defining norms for the identification of children with developmental language delay, or controlling for vocabulary ability while studying other developmental domains). Thus, in scenarios where bilingual and monolingual children are directly compared, our findings suggest that bilingual children should be assessed using conceptual vocabularies to ensure comparability. Conceptual vocabularies were consistently the most similar to monolingual vocabularies across a range of assessment conditions, and would therefore reduce the measurement inequivalences between bilingual and monolingual samples. Nonetheless, we recommend caution when comparing bilingual and monolingual samples, as many other features of vocabulary development may be dissimilar between the two, including the diagnostic accuracy of vocabulary measurements for atypical language development (De Houwer, 2023; Rothman et al., 2023). This evidence points to several directions for future work. First, studies should report vocabulary in both languages, together with information about translation equivalents.

Conceptual scoring needs to be applied to direct, standardized tests beyond 6 years of age, the range where our data were sparsest. Receptive and expressive vocabulary should be measured in the same children so that the effect of domain can be separated from differences between samples. Also, testing language distance properly requires sampling language pairs across a much wider range of typological distance than the English-centered pairs available (Blom et al., 2019; Floccia et al., 2018). The null effects of developmental status and language distance should be read as gaps in the evidence rather than as evidence that these factors do not matter.

Finally, in clinical contexts, our dataset had no direct contrasts between monolingual vocabulary and either conceptual or total vocabulary.

We also highlight two observations about the state of bilingualism research. First, we found that the distributions of investigated languages and language pairs were heavily rightskewed, with very little representation of non-Indo-European languages, or language pairs not including English as one of the two languages. Thus, the generalizability of our findings remains unknown; for example, very few of the included studies investigated bilinguals learning languages of Africa, or two closely related languages, which may result in different patterns of word learning in comparison with bilinguals learning very dissimilar languages (Blom et al., 2019), and therefore differential effects on vocabulary measurements. Claims about language acquisition that are purported to be universally true across all children must be able to account for language learning trajectories across the vast range of linguistic contexts that exist, and thus a much more comprehensive and equitable representation of populations is crucial for the continued advancement of language acquisition research.

Second, we recommend more detailed reporting of participants' linguistic backgrounds to better aid results interpretation. Multilingualism is extremely heterogeneous (e.g., which caregivers speak which languages, whether languages are spoken in the community or are heritage languages, or the perceived status of languages); as such, greater clarity about the language contexts is crucial in studies of multilingual children. In particular, studies that employed single-language vocabularies varied in which language was chosen: often, the assessed language was the language spoken in the community or a convenience language, whereas it may also have been the dominant language of the child, defined by parent report, relative language exposure, or vocabulary performance itself. We note that underreporting of how this single language was chosen prohibited more fine-grained testing of how different single-language choices influence the observed vocabulary comparisons. Other key factors such as the relative exposure of children to each language were also not codable because of data sparsity. We encourage language acquisition researchers to provide more information about the language experiences of their samples, so as to more explicitly describe possible contextual factors that may affect children's language outcomes.

Limitations

It is important to note that the studies included in our meta-analysis exhibit significant heterogeneity in terms of the population (e.g., languages spoken by children, participants' age), the assessment (between analyses across monolinguals and bilinguals, within analysis on bilingual children, assessment procedures), and the outcome (e.g., language domains, vocabulary measure, raw or standardized scores). Although we investigated the possible moderating effect of some of these variables, there were many other dimensions of heterogeneity that we could not capture due to partial or unreported information, which may limit the generalizability of our results to a broader set of contexts and samples. Nonetheless, our key findings appeared to be relatively robust to variation in our studied moderators; future studies focused on other dimensions of variation can help to shed more light on the stability of our observed effects.

Additionally, the quality of a meta-analysis necessarily depends on the quality of the studies included. Indeed, Egger's test revealed some evidence for small-study effects for singlelanguage and conceptual vocabularies specifically, which may indicate publication bias.

However, the possible effects of bias are mitigated by the fact that many of our studies had vocabulary measurements as a covariate in the original study, rather than as the key outcome of interest. As such, we considered it less likely that the findings were notably affected by researcher and publication biases.

Conclusion

The current network meta-regression revealed that bilingual conceptual vocabularies were the most commensurate with comparative monolingual vocabularies-this comparison showed no reliable difference in magnitude across ages, vocabulary domains, and instrument types. We further encourage researchers to expand the range of bilingual contexts studied, and to provide greater detail about the linguistic environments of multilingual samples to support more accurate inferences and generalizations about language acquisition phenomena in bilingual children. These findings have possible implications for clinical applications as well as experimental research, and further work exploring underrepresented populations (e.g., understudied language pairs, atypically developing children) will help to better clarify the vocabulary trajectories of young learners of multiple languages.

Supplemental material

Appendix A. PRISMA flow diagram Figure A1 shows the PRISMA flow diagram for the network meta-analysis. We note that many of the studies excluded due to wrong study design were not eligible for inclusion because they did not contain a comparison of interest (either a bilingual versus monolingual comparison, or a comparison among different vocabulary measures for bilinguals).

Appendix B. Network meta-analysis model formulation.

We fitted a Bayesian network meta-analysis with four nodes: monolingual vocabulary (Mono), bilingual single-language vocabulary (Bi-SL), bilingual total vocabulary (Bi-TV), and bilingual conceptual vocabulary (Bi-CV). Mono was used as the network reference, and effects were represented as contrasts between nodes, operationalized as standardized mean differences calculated as Hedges' g. We term the set of bilingual nodes Bi = {Bi-SL, Bi-TV, Bi-CV }.

The expected value of a single contrast is: where A a i , j i , c i is the latent node-level effect for node a, study j, and participant cohort c, and β a represents the meta-regression coefficients for covariates x i .

T represents the "treatment" node and R represents the "reference" node; typically, the reference node is the monolingual node where available, but if only within-bilingual comparisons were included in a study, then the treatment and reference nodes are two different bilingual vocabulary measurements.

The latent node-level effect is defined as:

A a , j , c =d a +δ j , a +u c , a +v c where d a is the population-average basic node-level effect, δ j , a is the study-specific deviation, u c , a is the bilingual group-specific cohort deviation, and v c is the scalar cohort effect.

d a , δ j , a , and u c , a are defined relative to the monolingual reference node; thus, they are equal to zero when a=¿ Mono, and are equal to a relative bilingual minus monolingual effect for a ∈ Bi.

The prior for d a is as follows:

Study type. We included experimental, quasi-experimental, and observational studies, and excluded opinion and review articles.In sum, studies included in the systematic review should a) include direct and/or indirect measurements of receptive and/or expressive vocabulary in the languages spoken by the child, b) compare bilingual lexical data to monolingual data (in at least one of the languages spoken by the bilingual sample) and/or compare different vocabulary measures for bilingual children (total vocabulary, conceptual vocabulary, or single-language vocabulary).
